attribution.note: Co-written post (with Davis) published on Marcus's own Substack in the authors' voice. Marcus endorses it.

semantics.note: Matches both sentences. 'These benchmarks' most naturally means Davis's surveyed collection of 100+ benchmarks; the normalisation widens this a little to 'existing benchmarks'. That is acceptable.

contract.note: The contract's readings of 'most forms', 'good reliable' and the coverage union are ordinary and fair. Neither 'most forms' nor 'reliable' has a stated measure, though, so the result depends on the evaluator's taxonomy and validation standard.

evidence.note: SpartQA (2021) shows that some spatial reasoning was benchmarked. That does not contradict the claim that most forms went untested.
PIQA (2019) is one physical commonsense benchmark. It does not establish coverage of most forms or a validated broad measure.
A Dec 2023 survey, after the post, notes much 'unexplored terrain'. It covers a later inventory and does not quantify coverage at Feb 2023.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet is an independent audit of the Feb 2023 inventory's coverage of spatial and physical reasoning categories, or a validation study of broad commonsense measures. The individual benchmarks show partial coverage only, and the later survey points to remaining gaps but covers a different period. The packet does not settle the outcome.

attribution.note: Co-written post on Marcus's Substack, stated in the authors' own voice.

semantics.note: The 'DO ask' half is normative. The drafter rightly takes out the descriptive half: weaknesses in time, space and human interactions are many and critical.

contract.note: Reading 'critical' as materially limiting is ordinary, and the 2022 to Feb 2023 window is reasonable. The support condition needs weaknesses in all three domains, so whether the claim is read collectively or per domain affects the result.

evidence.note: Bang et al. (Feb 2023): ChatGPT 'lacks spatial reasoning' (63% on spatial relations; 5 of 20 clock questions). Temporal reasoning was better (26 of 30), which weakens the claim for time.
Sap et al. (Oct 2022): GPT-3 got 55% on SocialIQa, more than 30 points below humans, and peaked at 60% on mental-state questions. This supports interpersonal weaknesses.
Kosinski v2 (Feb 2023): davinci-003 solved 93% of false-belief tasks. This partly cuts against interpersonal weakness for newer models, but the task set is narrow.

reviews.rationale: Spatial weakness is well supported (e1). Interpersonal weakness is supported for GPT-3 (e2), though the newer model's strong false-belief results temper it (e3). For time, the one contemporary evaluation found comparatively good performance (26 of 30), so 'many and critical' weaknesses there are not shown. The spatial and social parts hold; the temporal part does not.

attribution.note: Co-written post on Marcus's Substack, stated in the authors' own voice.

semantics.note: Revision 2 correctly restores the scope (LLMs and other ML systems such as MT) and the release aside, and leaves out the separate 'may well' hedge.

contract.note: Fair plain reading: better overall but with regressions on some tasks. Treating the release-practice aside as secondary and untested is reasonable. Developer papers are allowed sources under the contract.

evidence.note: OpenAI's InstructGPT paper reports regressions against GPT-3 on SQuAD, DROP, HellaSwag and WMT Fr-En, alongside overall preference gains. It is a company disclosure, but the admission runs against the company's interest.
The abstract reports human preference and truthfulness gains alongside 'minimal' regressions on public NLP datasets, which fits the improved-overall-but-not-everywhere pattern.

reviews.rationale: The InstructGPT paper documents what the contract's support condition asks for: a newer GPT-3 line model that is better overall but regresses on specific benchmarks, including machine translation. The packet has no counterevidence. The aside that unimproved versions are never released is not verified, and the evidence covers only OpenAI.
